cues.text: Let us turn to network topology and how we select one.
Start with a distinction that people often blur.
Physical topology describes the physical arrangement of the network: where the devices sit and how the cables or links actually connect them.
Logical topology describes the communication paths, meaning how data actually travels between devices.
The two can differ, so when someone asks what topology a network uses, you should first ask which of the two they mean.
Now let us compare the main topologies.
The table has four columns: the topology, its layout, its strength, and its weakness.
We will take the rows in order.
First, the bus topology.
Its layout is a shared backbone, a single common cable that every device attaches to.
Its strength is low cable cost, because one backbone serves everyone.
Its weakness is that it has a shared failure and collision domain, and it scales poorly.
Because everything shares one medium, a fault affects the devices on it together, and the devices compete for the same medium, which is what a shared collision domain means.
As you add devices, this sharing becomes harder to manage.
Second, the star topology.
Here the devices connect to a central switch.
Its strength is easy isolation and expansion.
Each device has its own link to the switch, so a problem with one device's connection can be isolated, and adding a device means adding one more connection.
Its weakness is central switch failure, unless the switch is made redundant.
If that one central switch fails, the devices that depend on it lose connectivity, so the center needs protecting with redundancy.
Third, the ring topology.
In a ring, each node is connected to its neighbours.
Its strength is predictable paths in some designs, because traffic follows a defined route around the ring.
Its weakness is that a break can disrupt a single ring.
Note the qualifications: the predictability applies in some designs, and the disruption concerns a single ring.
Fourth, the mesh topology.
Its layout is multiple interconnections between devices.
Its strength is alternative paths and resilience: if one path fails, another may be available.
Its weakness is higher link cost and complexity, since more links mean more to buy, install and manage.
Fifth, the tree topology.
This is hierarchical stars, with stars arranged in tiers.
Its strength is structured campus expansion, because a campus network can grow tier by tier in an organised way.
Its weakness is upper-tier dependency: the lower tiers depend on the tiers above them, so a problem higher up affects what is beneath it.
Sixth, the hybrid topology.
This is a combination of patterns, mixing the designs we have just seen.
Its strength is that it balances resilience and cost.
Its weakness is that it requires careful design, because combining patterns only works well if the combination is planned deliberately.
Next, some important points about meshes and resilience.
A full mesh of n devices needs n times n minus one, divided by two, undirected links.
The formula is n(n−1)/2.
Here n is the number of devices, and each link is undirected, meaning one link between two devices counts once, not once per direction.
Let us apply it to the source's example: with 6 devices, n is 6, so n minus one is 5.
Six times five is 30, and thirty divided by two is 15.
So 6 devices need 15 links, which matches the source.
Notice how the link count grows quickly as devices are added, and that is the cost and complexity weakness we saw in the table.
A partial mesh can protect critical paths without connecting every pair.
Instead of linking every device to every other, you add extra links only where an outage would matter most, which gives protection at lower cost than a full mesh.
Now two terms that are easy to confuse.
A switched star separates collision domains.
VLANs separate broadcast domains.
These are different mechanisms doing different jobs: the switched star addresses collisions, and VLANs address broadcasts.
Finally, redundant Ethernet paths need loop avoidance, such as spanning tree or routed links.
If you create more than one Ethernet path between points, you must prevent loops, and the source names spanning tree and routed links as ways to do so.
And the closing caution: more links alone do not guarantee resilience.

Adding links is not enough by itself, because, as we just saw, redundant Ethernet paths need loop avoidance, and a topology has to be designed deliberately to deliver the resilience it appears to promise.
